Area · Core processes

Memory

How we store, keep and retrieve information, why we forget and why we sometimes remember things that did not happen that way.

Level 1 · Short introduction

Memory is not a filing cabinet of exact copies. It is a set of systems that encode information (prepare it for storage), store it and retrieve it when needed. Each memory is partly rebuilt every time we recall it. That is why we forget, mix up details and sometimes confidently remember things that did not happen that way.

Level 2 · Fuller explanation

Kinds of memory

  • Sensory memory: lasts fractions of a second and holds a brief trace of what we see or hear.
  • Working memory: the mental space where we hold and manipulate information while using it, like a phone number we keep repeating. Its capacity is small, about four meaningful items.
  • Long-term memory, usually divided into:
    • episodic: memories of lived situations (what I had for dinner yesterday, my first day at work);
    • semantic: general knowledge (Paris is the capital of France);
    • procedural: skills (riding a bike), used without remembering how we learned them.

Why we forget

Hermann Ebbinghaus learned lists of nonsense syllables and measured how hard it was to relearn them as time passed. His forgetting curve (1885) shows a steep early drop that later levels off. We forget because information was poorly encoded, because other memories interfere, or because we lack the right cue to retrieve it.

Remembering is reconstructing

In the 1930s Frederic Bartlett asked English students to recall a traditional Native American story. With each retelling the text grew shorter and was adapted to what felt familiar to them. Decades later, Elizabeth Loftus showed that the wording of a question can change a memory.

What helps us remember

  • Retrieval practice: trying to recall (testing yourself) works better than rereading.
  • Spacing study over several sessions instead of cramming.
  • Making meaning: linking the new to what we already know.
  • Sleep: sleep takes part in consolidating what we have learned.

Working memory

In 1974 Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch proposed that short-term memory is not a simple store but a working system with several parts: a phonological loop that rehearses sounds and words, a visuospatial sketchpad for images and positions, and a central executive that allocates attention. In 2000 Baddeley added an "episodic buffer" that integrates information. Its capacity is small, which is why long instructions and complex mental arithmetic are hard.

Memory and emotion

Emotionally charged events are remembered better, partly because the amygdala strengthens consolidation in the hippocampus. But remembering them more vividly does not mean remembering them more accurately: flashbulb memories, such as where we were on 11 September 2001, change over the years even though we feel very sure of them.

Prospective memory

We do not only remember the past: we also have to remember to do things in the future, such as taking a pill or phoning someone. This is prospective memory, and it often fails. External aids (alarms, notes, leaving things in sight) are perfectly legitimate strategies.

Why don't we remember being babies?

Almost nobody remembers anything from before the age of three or four. This is infantile amnesia. It is not that babies do not learn: they recognise faces, voices and routines. What is missing are lasting episodic memories, the kind that can be placed in a time and place. Contributing factors are thought to include the maturation of the hippocampus, the development of language and of a sense of "self" to which experiences can belong, and the many new neurons formed in those years, which reorganise connections. Many "first memories" are really reconstructions from photos and family stories.

Memory as we age

With age, not everything declines equally. Processing speed, working memory and the ability to recall specific episodes decrease, especially without cues. Vocabulary and general knowledge, on the other hand, are maintained or even improve into late life, as do well-practised skills. Forgetting a name and recalling it later is normal. More worrying signs are getting lost in familiar places, asking the same question repeatedly within a short time, or new difficulties managing money or medication: these are worth having checked.

Places and maps in the brain

In 1971, John O'Keefe discovered place cells in the rat hippocampus, neurons that fire when the animal is in a particular spot. Later, May-Britt and Edvard Moser found grid cells, which form a kind of coordinate system. All three received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2014. In humans, Eleanor Maguire showed that London taxi drivers, who memorise thousands of streets, have a larger posterior hippocampus than other people.

Level 3 · Going further, with references

The case of Henry Molaison (known for decades as H. M.) was decisive. In 1953 parts of both medial temporal lobes were removed to treat severe epilepsy. Afterwards he could not form new lasting episodic memories, but, as Brenda Milner showed, he did improve at motor tasks such as mirror drawing, even though he did not remember practising them. It was evidence that distinct memory systems exist and of the importance of the hippocampus.

The most cited models are Atkinson and Shiffrin's modal model (1968), which separated sensory, short-term and long-term stores, and Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model (1974), with a central executive, a phonological loop and a visuospatial sketchpad (Baddeley later added an episodic buffer). Endel Tulving proposed the distinction between episodic and semantic memory in 1972.

In education, the retrieval practice effect (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006) and the spacing effect are among the most replicated findings. Research on eyewitness testimony has changed police and court procedures in several countries.

Open debates: exactly how memory systems relate in the brain; what happens when a memory is reconsolidated after being recalled; and how far laboratory results on false memories apply to traumatic experiences.

Reconsolidation

For a long time it was thought that once consolidated, a memory was fixed. In 2000 Karim Nader and colleagues showed in rats that reactivating a fear memory makes it unstable for a while, so that it needs to be "reconsolidated". Researchers are exploring whether this window can be used to treat traumatic memories or addictions, with results that are still preliminary.

Exceptional memories

Some people with highly superior autobiographical memory remember what they did on almost any day of their lives since adolescence, as James McGaugh's group described in 2006. Curiously, they are usually no better than average at memorising lists, and they are also vulnerable to false memories. The opposite exists too: healthy people with very poor autobiographical memory.

Memory and witnesses

Eyewitness identifications are among the most common causes of wrongful convictions later overturned by DNA evidence. Research has shown that the confidence with which a witness identifies someone at trial says little, because it grows over time and with later conversations. What does carry weight is confidence at the first identification, made under good conditions. That is why it is recommended that line-ups be run by someone who does not know who the suspect is and that the witness's confidence be recorded immediately.

Remembering the future

Patients with severe amnesia from hippocampal damage not only struggle to recall their past: they also find it hard to imagine future scenes in detail. This led Daniel Schacter and others to propose that episodic memory serves above all to build simulations of what might happen. Remembering would be recombining fragments, and the same flexibility that lets us plan is what makes us vulnerable to false memories.
